meta.title: Lucian Andrei Negoita — Solutions Architect
meta.description: Cloud and applications solutions architect in Spain. I design APIs, service boundaries and the decisions that hold them together. Currently at Capgemini Invent, for an IBEX 35 multinational energy company.

hero.greeting: Hola, soy Lucian. I make software behave itself
hero.lead: I design application and cloud architecture: where each boundary goes, why, and what happens when it fails. Then I write the code on both sides of it.
hero.now: Solutions Architect at Capgemini Invent, for an IBEX 35 multinational energy company.

work.title: Where I've been
work.subtitle: so far
work.flowSubtitle: from a request to something running

about.title: A bit about me
about.body: I studied medicine for four years before switching to computer engineering. It turns out both are the same job: reading a system you did not design, and working out what is actually wrong with it.

contact.title: Let's build something
contact.body: Write to me. I answer everything, usually the same day.

education.title: M.Sc. in Big Data and Cloud Computing, UCLM
education.body: Cloud on AWS with containers, serverless and autoscaling. Data architecture (Data Lake, Lakehouse, Mesh), processing with Spark and Hadoop on EMR, Databricks and Dataproc, streaming with Kafka and Spark Structured Streaming, MLOps and data governance.

education.title: B.Sc. in Computer Engineering, UCLM
education.body: Bilingual track. Highest honours (Matrícula de Honor) in Web and Services Engineering; final thesis nominated for highest honours.

education.title: Advanced Course in Digital Tools for Transport and Logistics, UCLM
education.body: 15 ECTS university course from the School of Computer Engineering in Albacete. Agile project management (Scrum, Kanban), cloud computing on AWS (EC2, S3, Lambda), artificial intelligence and machine learning, business intelligence, big data analytics, robotics, blockchain and smart contracts, and cybersecurity, applied to transport and logistics.

experience.summary: I design and review web, mobile and cloud application architectures in the Development Architecture Service of an IBEX 35 multinational energy company, and document every decision for the teams that build them.

client.name: Multinational energy company
client.body: An IBEX 35 multinational energy company. I work inside its Development Architecture Service.

experience.statement: My job is to decide where one service ends and the next begins — and to leave behind a written reason for every line I draw.

duties.title: Design the solution
duties.body: Architectures for custom builds (Vue, C#, Node.js) and low-code (OutSystems) on Azure and AWS: authentication, persistence, integration and asynchronous processing, with scalability, availability and security in line with enterprise standards.

duties.title: Write it down
duties.body: Architecture documents (DSA), reasoned decisions and technical standards. Every design states the alternatives, the chosen one and how to implement it.

duties.title: Review and govern
duties.body: Architecture boards with the teams, and design and code reviews against the corporate quality and security gates.

duties.title: Proofs of concept
duties.body: Technical POCs to validate patterns before they become standards: Kubernetes deployments, database CI/CD and AI agents built into the development lifecycle.

flow.title: A need arrives
flow.body: A team needs data or behaviour that lives somewhere else.

flow.title: Options on the table
flow.body: Two or three ways to draw the boundary, each with a cost.

flow.title: The ADR
flow.body: One chosen, written down, with the reasoning attached.

flow.title: Review & ship
flow.body: Implementation reviewed against quality and security gates.

highlights: Corporate framework for adopting AI agents across the development lifecycle: RAG indexing of the architecture corpus, deployment model, access, security and integration.
Phase-based development standards across the lifecycle, covering pipelines, containers and security.
Solution designs (DSA) for custom and OutSystems applications on the corporate templates.

experience.summary: Built Spring Boot and Angular into a government platform the public actually uses, and kept its old JBoss half breathing while I did.

client.name: Public administration
client.body: A public-facing application: real users, real incidents, and a legacy code base underneath.

experience.statement: My first contact with software someone actually uses — nothing teaches faster than a production incident.

duties.title: Endpoints and schema
duties.body: Spring Boot REST endpoints on JPA/Hibernate, with the schema versioned in Liquibase so every change could be walked back.

duties.title: The interface on top
duties.body: Angular and TypeScript screens consuming those endpoints, built for people who do not choose to use the application.

duties.title: Keeping it standing
duties.body: I automated in Python the extraction and transformation of complex data (BLOB/CLOB) from legacy databases, and analysed the old Java/JBoss code to plan a migration with no data loss.

highlights: Python ETL for BLOB/CLOB types that replaced a manual, error-prone process.
Dependency map of the legacy Java code to plan the migration without losing data.

experience.summary: My own Linux servers, from empty box to running service. Nobody else on call at 3 a.m.

client.name: Myself
client.body: No team, no on-call rotation, nobody to escalate to. If it fell over, I was the one who woke up.

experience.statement: Running something alone teaches you one thing reading never does: what breaks first.

duties.title: Provision
duties.body: Linux servers from scratch: base system, networking, access and hardening.

duties.title: Deploy
duties.body: Getting services running and keeping them reproducible, so a deploy was not an act of faith.

duties.title: Watch and maintain
duties.body: Monitoring, updates, and the boring work that prevents the midnight phone call.

highlights: Ethereum mining rigs on HiveOS (Linux): monitoring, performance tuning and incident handling.

projectList.title: Mortgage Analyst
projectList.summary: Compares mortgages by what they cost in euros over the whole loan, not by APR.
projectList.lead: Mortgage comparison for the Spanish market that ranks offers by total cost in euros, under Euribor scenarios, including the cost of linked products and each region's purchase tax.
projectList.statement: Mortgages ranked by what they cost in euros

architecture.title: Banco de España
architecture.body: Euribor ingestion with rate limiting, raw copies and quarantine for implausible values.

architecture.title: Pure domain
architecture.body: Framework-free Java engine: French amortisation, IRR-based APR, bonifications and taxes.

architecture.title: PostgreSQL
architecture.body: Offers versioned with SCD2 and schema in Liquibase. Every old quote stays reproducible.

architecture.title: Angular
architecture.body: Shows the ranking and flags which figures are estimates. It computes nothing.

projectList.archSubtitle: ports and adapters, checked on every build
projectList.why: APR is misleading for variable and mixed mortgages: the regulation computes it with Euribor frozen. A bonified APR can also cost more in euros when the insurance the bank requires costs more than the interest it saves. I wanted a tool that answers the real question: how much will I pay.
learned: Architecture rules only count when they break the build. ArchUnit forbids double for money and Spring imports in the domain.
Testcontainers caught a bug no review would have seen: a Hibernate timezone property shifted the end-of-validity sentinel by one hour.
Every figure that comes from a statute carries its legal reference in the database, validated at startup.

projectList.title: LucyERP
projectList.summary: ERP for aesthetic clinics: room scheduling, sales, stock and cash register, with WhatsApp reminders.
projectList.lead: Handles room-based scheduling, clients, sales, stock and the cash register of an aesthetic clinic, and sends automatic appointment reminders through WhatsApp.
projectList.statement: An ERP that lives on the clinic's PC

architecture.title: Front desk
architecture.body: Scheduling by room and staff, client records and daily cash.

architecture.title: Next.js standalone
architecture.body: App and API in a single Node server, with Prisma over one SQLite file.

architecture.title: Worker
architecture.body: A node-cron process that schedules the reminders.

architecture.title: WhatsApp Cloud API
architecture.body: Appointment reminders to clients.

projectList.why: A small clinic does not need a monthly SaaS subscription or a server to maintain. It needs something that runs on the front-desk computer, works without internet and whose data fits on a USB stick.
learned: Deploying on-premise forces you to think about what the cloud gives you for free: a Windows service, backups and schema upgrades without data loss.
SQLite is a very serious database when there is a single writer.

projectList.title: Relay Traffic Copilot
projectList.summary: AI copilot that scores Amazon Relay load offers by real profit per km and drafts how to negotiate them.
projectList.lead: Copilot for a self-employed haulier working with Amazon Relay. It reads offers from email, computes the real profit per km including empty legs and drafts a negotiation reply in Spanish and English.
projectList.statement: The AI recommends, the driver decides

architecture.title: Gmail
architecture.body: Picks up load offers every few minutes.

architecture.title: Evaluator
architecture.body: Three-block cost model, official diesel price and a six-level rating.

architecture.title: Claude
architecture.body: Drafts the counter-offer in Spanish and English and adapts strategy to the season.

architecture.title: Flask dashboard
architecture.body: Nothing is sent or accepted without human approval.

projectList.archSubtitle: with human approval at every step
projectList.why: I built it for a relative who drives a truck. The per-km price the platform shows ignores the empty drive to the pickup and the real cost of the truck, and choosing in a hurry among dozens of offers a day costs money.
learned: The most important rule in the system is a constraint: the AI never acts on its own.
Keeping the AI client in a single module made it possible to switch providers without touching the rest of the code.

projectList.title: peaje
projectList.summary: Self-hosted proxy that accounts LLM spend per request and cuts off hard when the budget runs out.
projectList.lead: Sits between coding agents and LLM providers, records the exact cost of every request and enforces hard per-key budgets. One Go binary, zero dependencies, backed by SQLite.
projectList.statement: spent + held ≤ budget, at every instant

architecture.title: Coding agent
architecture.body: Claude Code, Cursor or any compatible client.

architecture.title: Reserve
architecture.body: Before forwarding, it reserves the maximum possible cost against the budget.

architecture.title: Provider
architecture.body: The SSE stream flows unbuffered. Real cost comes from the provider's usage field.

architecture.title: Settle
architecture.body: Settles exactly once over a crash-safe journal.

projectList.why: Teams adopting coding agents find out their spend on the invoice, a month late. Billing APIs lag 24 to 48 hours, and gateways that track cost do it without guarantees exactly where the money is: between admission and settlement of concurrent requests.
learned: Money is stored as integers (micro-USD), never floating point.
I write the ledger core by hand. It is the part I need to defend line by line.

projectList.title: Real-time collaborative editor
projectList.summary: Real-time collaborative coding inside Moodle, with CRDTs and events on Kafka.
projectList.lead: My final degree project: several people edit the same code at once inside a Moodle course, with no conflicts and every change published as an event.
projectList.statement: Many people, one file, zero conflicts

architecture.title: Moodle plugin
architecture.body: The editor lives inside the course, with Moodle's users and permissions.

architecture.title: Hocuspocus + Yjs
architecture.body: Syncs edits with CRDTs over WebSocket.

architecture.title: Kafka
architecture.body: Every change is published as an event for processing.

architecture.title: Selenium
architecture.body: E2E tests with up to 10 users editing at once.

projectList.archSubtitle: CRDTs and events, end to end
projectList.why: I wanted a real distributed systems problem: concurrent editing where latency and event order matter, built into a platform students already use.
learned: CRDTs solve convergence, but not presence or permissions: those need their own design.
Testing with 10 real browsers at once teaches more than any unit test.

projectList.title: Serverless data pipeline
projectList.summary: Files land in S3, Lambda reshapes them, DynamoDB hands them back — near-real time, no servers to babysit.
projectList.lead: Files land in a bucket, code wakes up, reshapes them, and puts them somewhere a dashboard can read in near-real time. Nothing runs when nothing happens.
projectList.statement: A pipeline with no servers to babysit

architecture.title: S3 bucket
architecture.body: A raw file arrives. That is the only trigger.

architecture.title: Lambda
architecture.body: Validates, reshapes, enriches. Scales to zero between events.

architecture.title: DynamoDB
architecture.body: Written so the read pattern is cheap, not so the writes are pretty.

architecture.title: Whoever asks
architecture.body: Near-real-time answers instead of a nightly batch.

projectList.why: I wanted to understand event-driven architecture by paying for it, not by reading about it. A nightly batch job is easy. Something that reacts the moment a file lands, costs nothing while idle, and still behaves when two files arrive at once — that is where the real decisions are.
learned: In DynamoDB you design the table around the question you will ask, not the data you have.
A retry that is not idempotent is just a slower way to corrupt your data.
Writing the runbook first made the architecture simpler — anything I could not explain, I removed.
